title: Udaypur: A Small Town with a Long Memory

sections.title: The village under the temple
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows that today's Udaypur is a large, ordinary village living inside the gateways, lanes and memories of a much greater medieval town. Its residents keep the founder's name and his temple in worship, but hold little of the history.
sections.transition: The name the village keeps is a king's. The next section asks whose kingdom this was and why its king put his name here.

paras.first: On the road from Ganj Basoda, hillocks begin to dot the horizon almost ten kilometres out, and two of them belong to Udaypur; nearer the village, one proves to be the big cylindrical hill known for its shape as Shiv pindi.
paras.last: Its surviving monuments, Hindu and Muslim, are what remains of that medieval town.
paras.plan_point: Make the reader meet Udaypur in the order anyone coming from Ganj Basoda does: the hills, then the temple, then the village. By the end of the paragraph the reader should sense a place that once mattered, without being told so twice. Vijay Manohar Tiwari is named once here, as the eyewitness: use the item for Tiwari's sight of the temple, never for a distance (testimony never supplies a measurement). Roads, the railway station and distances are context, at most one clause: this is an approach, not a location list. (Plan note, run 2, 15 October.)

paras.first: The place has kept the character of a village.
paras.last: In 1979 it had primary and higher secondary schools, Ayurvedic and veterinary dispensaries and a post office, and a market met every Monday.
paras.plan_point: The census village (people, houses, schools, a weekly market) is ordinary. Its scale, not its antiquity, is the first thing that needs explaining.

paras.first: Within a fortified wall with several gates and watch towers, an area of a few acres still known as the walled city held palaces, temples, open spaces and a triple gateway, Teen Darwaza, leading to a royal square; the gates still stand, but the wall survives only in broken stretches.
paras.last: One family still uses a house spread across twelve courtyards, most of them in ruins; its entrance, under a stone balcony, opens into a central court with a temple on the north, and old sculptures lie among its ruined parts.
paras.plan_point: Residents have built their houses against the old gateways and trade beside rubble-filled rows, so the medieval plan still shapes where Udaypur walks and trades. Residents are the agents.

paras.first: Near the temple stands Ghariyālon Kā Makān, the house of the temple’s time-keepers, a family that claims to have been there for centuries.
paras.last: A shorter account has only a thread across the reservoir, broken by someone, a fall and a death, and makes the spot her *samādhi*, a memorial to her; Tiwari does not know how long that story has been current.
paras.plan_title: Memories that point to the founder
paras.plan_point: Where village memory touches the temple and its water, it reaches back to Udayāditya: the time-keepers' house, the remembered tally of waterworks, the fields remembered as his tank, and the Berni Mata stories that place a dancer in his court. These are memory, told as memory. The yakṣa reading goes in a note.

paras.first: The eleventh-century Udayeśvara temple faces east inside a walled court that probably had an entrance at each cardinal point, and the Archaeological Survey of India now protects it.
paras.last: Of how Udayāditya’s name came to the place, tradition keeps a hunting story: the king came upon a snake surrounded by fire and afterwards built a city and a temple there and named them after himself.
paras.plan_title: A shrine, and a name others have borrowed
paras.plan_point: The temple lives as a shrine (daily worship, a fair, reverence across communities) more than as a record. The name the village keeps is overshadowed by Rajasthan's Udaipur and punned on locally. Close on the gap between what the village holds and what the place once was, without announcing what follows.

sections.title: A king's town on Malwa's eastern edge
sections.plan_title: A king's town on Malwa's eastern edge
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows the Paramāras as a kingdom, not an adjective. It was ruled from Dhārā, reached Bhilsa on the east, was nearly lost at Bhoja's death and was recovered by Udayāditya, a kinsman of Bhoja whose exact relationship is disputed. That king gave one name to a town, a temple and a tank on the kingdom's eastern edge, and the town served, in his reign, as the seat of a local house under the king, and in the 1160s–70s, under the Caulukyas, as the seat of an eastern division (R4, U1). Chapter 4 tells the full story; this section gives what the reader needs now.
sections.transition: The kingdom that made the town outlived its founder by two centuries, and every regime after it built inside his precinct.

paras.first: The Paramāras styled themselves lords of Malwa or kings of Avanti, and were known as rulers of Ujjain and of Dhārā.
paras.last: Udaypur was among the towns that grew under Paramāra rule.
paras.plan_point: Who the Paramāras were as a polity: lords of Malwa ruling from Dhārā, a kingdom whose eastern reach ran to Bhilsa. Udaypur lies at that eastern edge.

paras.first: The kingdom nearly ended with Bhoja.
paras.last: Under him the kingdom again stretched at least to Jhalrapatan in the north, Bhilsa in the east and Nimar in the south, almost the whole of Bhoja’s late territory, and Kalacuri inscriptions call him king of Malwa and lord of Dhārā.
paras.plan_point: Narrate the crisis. Bhoja died at war and his enemies took Dhārā. Jayasiṃha regained the throne with Chālukya help, then died fighting new invaders. Udayāditya recovered the kingdom. His kinship to Bhoja is disputed: give the canon wording, with one note setting out the readings by tier (the praśasti names him only as successor; the Nagpur inscription calls him *bandhu*, "a relative in general"; the Dongargaon and Jainad inscriptions make him a brother; a sixteenth-century genealogy, rejected by its editor; later "cousin or brother" and "nephew"). The accession is c. 1070, the working position, with the other datings beside it in a note. The Nagpur verse's boar image is the dynasty's own telling.

paras.first: An inscription on the temple credits Udayāditya with founding a town, building a temple of Śiva and excavating a tank, and with naming all three after himself: Udayapura, Udayeśvara and Udayasamudra.
paras.last: The question bears on whether Udaypur began as the seat of a lord on his way to the throne or as a new king’s undertaking.
paras.plan_title: One name for a town, a temple and a tank
paras.plan_point: The founding was an act of naming as much as of building: Udayapura, Udayeśvara and Udayasamudra under one name, with work read as begun in V.S. 1116 (a reading: R1, R3) and a flag raised in 1080. Whether 1059 falls before his kingship changes what kind of founding it was: a lord's seat in his rise, or a new king's first work. State that once.

paras.first: The town’s place in the kingdom shows in how the kingdom was governed.
paras.last: If that reading holds, the town that bore a king’s name may also have been the seat of a local house holding it under him.
paras.plan_point: Explain what "a seat of the eastern division" meant. The kingdom was organised into maṇḍalas, bhogas, viṣayas and pathakas under viceroys and local officers. In a record of the early 1170s Udayapura lies in the Bhāillasvāmi-mahādvādaśaka, and in the 1160s it was a headquarters of the eastern division under the Caulukyas (R4, U1); and its own inscription calls it the capital of the Nēmaka house under the king: a royal name over a local line's seat. Ganguly's reading of a feudatory line at Udayapur is attributed to him.

sections.title: Eight centuries in one precinct
sections.statement: By the end, the reader can place Udaypur's layers in time: - later Paramāra governors and kings at the town; - a Candella king at Bhilsa in 1134; - Paramāra rule in the east into the 1260s; - the conquest of Malwa in 1305; - the 1330s mosque in the temple court; - Mandu and Mughal building; - the Scindia brass; - the state's custody today. Through all of it the founder's temple stayed in worship.
sections.transition: What survives of the founder's own voice is a broken slab of praise, and how the place is known is the next question.

paras.first: The Paramāra kingdom did not stay whole.
paras.last: His son Jayavarman still held Bhilsa in 1263, and in 1269 Pathari, about 55 km farther north by east.
paras.plan_point: The east stayed contested after the founder. - Udayāditya's line lost Malwa to Gujarat under Yaśovarman, and a Candella king issued a grant while residing at Bhāillasvāmin in 1134. - The Mahākumāra branch held on in the east. - Paramāra officials and kings still acted at Udaypur: Lūṇapasāka's grants of 1171–73 and Devapāla residing there. The Lūṇapasāka date variants go in a note. - Jayavarman II still held Bhilsa in 1263. Narrate it briefly. Chapter 10 tells the full story.

paras.first: That possession ended within two generations.
paras.last: Local tradition, by contrast, dates an order to raze the temple to 1325 and remembers that no more than part of the western hall became a mosque.
paras.plan_title: 1305 and the court of the temple
paras.plan_point: The Paramāra state in Malwa ended with the conquest of 1305. At Udaypur the stone record shows partial survival: the central temple was kept, while a corner shrine and the hall for reading the Vedas came down for a mosque of the 1330s. The legends of the same conquest speak only of what was saved. The builder of the mosque is remembered two ways (note).

paras.first: Hoshang Shah moved the capital of Malwa permanently from Dhārā to Mandu in 1405.
paras.last: Close to it lie the ruins of a spacious mansion in the early Mughal style, with fine stone *jālī* screens, probably the residence of the local governor in Mughal times, and a platform of tombs stands in front of the mosque.
paras.plan_point: Sultanate and Mughal building went on within the town the Paramāras had named: the walled circuit and gates, Sher Khan's mosque of 1488, the Shahi Masjid of 1632, and a probable governor's mansion by the temple. Each new order was added to the old town, not set apart from it. The palace's founder is disputed (note).

paras.first: Later patrons left their mark on the temple.
paras.last: Udayeśvara itself has been read as the fullest expression of the Bhūmija style that the Paramāras developed, and as the model later architects of Malwa followed.
paras.plan_title: From a Scindia general to the state
paras.plan_point: The patrons changed while the shrine stayed in worship: - a Scindia general's brass cover of 1775, its donor disputed in a note; - maintenance under the Scindias; - protection by archaeology and forest departments today. One attributed assessment of the temple as a model, with Ramgarh and Nemawar as its followers, fits here in a sentence.

sections.title: How Udaypur is known
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows the kinds of evidence behind the story and what each can bear: - the praśasti, the dynasty's self-portrait, broken and kept in Gwalior; - the two dated inscriptions; - eight centuries of pilgrims' writing on the stones; - scholarship since the 1870s; - the survival legends, which are memory.
sections.transition: These records and memories all begin with Udayāditya's name, but they cannot say whether he founded the place or renamed it.

paras.first: The dynasty’s complete genealogy comes from Udaypur, on two broken slabs.
paras.last: The tidy span of the temple plan’s caption, “1059—1080”, therefore claims more than the stones settle.
paras.plan_point: The praśasti is the dynasty's only complete genealogy, and it opens with a hero sprung from Vasiṣṭha's fire-altar on Mount Abu. It is also praise: its earliest names are missing elsewhere and its building claims are uncorroborated. Its two halves were found apart and now lie in Gwalior, undated (readings in a note). It shows the founder as the dynasty wished him seen.

paras.first: The stones also hold a longer record of people who came.
paras.last: Restoration under Gwalior State in the 1920s, and then under the ASI, may have reset one inscribed slab with its carved face turned inwards and its inscribed face outwards, the reverse of the usual arrangement.
paras.plan_point: Inscriptions in Sanskrit, Persian and Hindi across eight centuries show pilgrims and patrons kept coming. Their count goes in a note. Modern reading began late: the 1871–72 tour, the 1888 edition, and the second slab found in 1925–26 and abraded. Name the readers only where they act.

paras.first: Beside the inscriptions the town keeps stories that explain why the temple survived.
paras.last: These stories are memory, of the temple’s survival and of its building; none of them tells how the town began.
paras.plan_point: The survival legends turn a partial survival into a deliverance: - the wetted gunpowder; - Aurangzeb; - a temple built in a night; - treasure. The gunpowder miracle itself concedes that a hall became a mosque. They are evidence for memory, not for the events they tell.

unmatched_plan.title: Two dates
unmatched_plan.point: The founding has two fixed points, V.S. 1116 and V.S. 1137. The second is read three ways: the flag-staff erected, the flag hoisted or the flag-staff repaired. Before 1080 the town is reached only through proposals and tradition, so the tidy caption "1059–1080" claims more than the stones settle.

sections.title: Founded or taken over?
sections.statement: By the end, the reader understands why the founding question is genuine: - what the case for an older place rests on (proposals that point the same way, each uncertain); - what the case for a new town rests on (an absence, which its own proponent qualifies, and traditions that remember earlier masters only as people the founder defeated); - what each answer would mean for the kind of royal act Udaypur began with. The section ends on the ground both answers stand on, which leads into Chapter 2.
sections.transition: Chapter 2 turns to that ground: the Betwa valley's water, stone and seasons.

paras.first: South-east of the village, near a stone quarry still in work, lies the Bhujariya Talab, a natural water body.
paras.last: The tank, the inscription and the columns all point to a time before Udayāditya, and their agreement makes an older place on this ground a serious possibility, not a certainty.
paras.plan_title: The case for an older place
paras.plan_point: Present the survey's proposals: the hill inscription read tentatively and assigned to the eighth century; the Bhujariya Talab, which may belong to the eighth or ninth century, its embankment older than the Udaysagar; columns provisionally dated seventh–eighth century and reused; layers read back to the sixth century; the uncemented wall. They point the same way, which gives the case its weight, but each is a proposal, which keeps it a case rather than a finding. Grade confidence on each clause. Who proposes what goes in a note. Never merge the tentatively read two-line inscription with the survey's inscription that "remains to be deciphered".

paras.first: The case for a new town starts from a reported absence: no inscription of the Paramāra kings before Udayāditya has been found at Udaypur, and from that, with the evidence of the name itself, the town has been taken to have come into being only in his time.
paras.last: Both traditions remember an older place, and both remember it only as something the founder overcame: memory leans towards renaming, but it tells the story from the founder’s side.
paras.plan_point: The case for a new town rests on the absence of earlier Paramāra inscriptions. That absence cannot rule out a place under other masters, and its proponent allows an earlier frontier post. The traditions of Bhringraj and Bhringrajpur and of Gond rule remember those masters, but only as people the founder defeated: memory favours renaming while telling it from the founder's side. The Daśārṇa and Udayagiri associations belong to Chapter 3.

paras.first: The two answers describe different acts of rule.
paras.last: None of these later records speaks of the place before Udayāditya’s name was on it.
paras.plan_point: Set out what each answer would mean: - If Udayāditya founded Udaypur, it was a royal creation on the recovered kingdom's eastern edge, and its long memory is the memory of one eleventh-century project. - If he renamed it, the naming laid a king's name over an older place: appropriation or reorganisation, a political re-inscription. The later echoes (Udhapuram, the sixteenth-century praise, the record of 1513) all come after the act and cannot decide between the two. Do not inflate the uncertainty.

paras.first: Either way, stone is quarried today beside the older tank, and water was held in tanks of more than one age, the Bhujariya Talab, proposed as older than Udayāditya, and the Udaysagar, attributed to him.
paras.last: Whoever first lived here, under his rule or before it, had to make terms with that stone and that water.
paras.plan_title: The ground both answers stand on
paras.plan_point: Close briefly on what is common to both answers: the place sits on a hill of stone with tanks around it, older and newer. Whoever first lived here had to make terms with that ground. Lead into Chapter 2 by content; never claim the land caused the founding.

opening: On the road from Ganj Basoda, hillocks begin to dot the horizon almost ten kilometres out, and two of them belong to Udaypur; nearer the village, one proves to be the big cylindrical hill known for its shape as Shiv pindi.
closing: Whoever first lived here, under his rule or before it, had to make terms with that stone and that water.
